Helenius de Cock
hə-lā'nee-əs də kok
n. (Helenius de Cock, 1824–1894, son of Hendrik de Cock, minister and professor at the Theological School at Kampen)
Latinized Greek Helenius, from helene, a torch; de Cock, the cook.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Helenius de Cock was ten years old when his father was deposed and the congregation of Ulrum seceded, and he grew up in a persecuted church. He studied for the ministry under the Seceder pastors who trained men in their own homes before the churches had a school, served congregations in the Christian Seceded Reformed Church, and in 1854 became one of the first teachers of the Theological School at Kampen, where he taught for the rest of his working life. His loyalty was to the confessional and Dortian character of the Secession against both the national church it had left and the newer movement under Abraham Kuyper that it would join in 1892. Late in life he wrote the biography of his father, preserving the documents and memories of 1834 for a generation that had not suffered for them. He is an example of the second generation's calling, to hand on what the first generation recovered: “shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD” (Psa 78:4). His office was Paul's charge to Timothy, “commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also” (2Ti 2:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a professor as one who publicly teaches any science or branch of learning, and biography as the history of the life of a particular person.

expand to see more

PROFES'SOR, n. One that publicly teaches any science or branch of learning; particularly, an officer in a university, college or other seminary.

BIOG'RAPHY, n. The history of the life and character of a particular person.

POL'ITY, n. The form or constitution of the civil government of a nation or state; or the general fundamental principles of that form of government. Ecclesiastical polity, the government of the church.

Key Scripture

Psa 78:4 — "We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the LORD, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done."

2Ti 2:2 — "And the things that thou hast heard of me among many witnesses, the same commit thou to faithful men, who shall be able to teach others also."

Tit 1:9 — "Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught, that he may be able by sound doctrine both to exhort and to convince the gainsayers."

Mal 2:7 — "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

The son of the Secession, who taught the next generation what their fathers had suffered for.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The danger his life addresses is the ordinary one of the second generation, which inherits a costly recovery as a settled custom and soon cannot say why the fathers left. Psa 78:4 makes the transmission a duty, not a sentiment: “We will not hide them from their children” (Psa 78:4).

The principle to recover is that church history and church polity are not antiquarian subjects but means of fidelity. A minister must be “Holding fast the faithful word as he hath been taught” (Tit 1:9), and a seminary that forgets how its church came to exist will not long remember what it believes.
